name: Yara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think, and they don't have to match. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollis and Sons, a family builder with about thirty people, and we mostly refurbish schools and health clinics. A lot of it happens in the school holidays, so in summer I'm working ten-hour days ripping out old classrooms and fitting new partitions, doors and cupboards. In term time it's clinics, usually at night or weekends so the patients aren't disturbed. I keep my jobs in a paper diary with a pencil tucked in the spine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's always a different building, and I like Mr Hollis, who still comes round on Fridays with doughnuts. What wears me out is the night shifts in clinics, because I never sleep right after. And the paperwork they keep adding, the risk forms and the photos, which I do on the site tablet only because I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. Less to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get back to work. I don't really post online, I'm not a big phone person. At the site hut I'd probably just shrug and say I never thought it was going to fit a door anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's how I like it. Kerem drives buses, I fit doors, we've got about eight months saved and we're careful. I don't use AI and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, honestly. Keep working for Hollis, keep saving, maybe finally get the car fixed. If they brought some AI thing in for the risk forms I'd let somebody else learn it and ask them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Not even a little curious about the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My younger brother shows me things on his phone and I just nod. I like knowing exactly how a thing works, and with those I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kerem's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses still need drivers in this one, I'd think. Some of the timetabling might change. He'd complain about the app, that's about it.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's get back to work, and shrug in the site hut that I never thought it would fit a door. I don't really post online.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her, which is how she likes it. She and her bus-driver partner have about eight months saved, and she doesn't use AI and wouldn't start.
S0.do: Keeps working for the same family builder and keeps saving, maybe gets the car fixed. Lets someone else learn any new AI tool for risk forms and asks them for help.
S0.quote: I like knowing exactly how a thing works, and with those I don't.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is content, practical and uninterested in AI, preferring things she can understand fully. Her life is built around a stable small employer and careful saving. She shows little politics, just a wish to be left to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. A few years of change. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some changes are probably sensible, and some will be silly, and we'll see which is which. I'm not against it, I'm just not first in the queue. I'd say that at work if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think refurbishment is messy enough that it'll take a long time for machines to manage it. Every old school is crooked in a different way. But firms like Hollis might get squeezed by big companies with machines, and that's what would worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd let the others try the new gadgets first and pick them up if I really had to. I'd keep saving the same amount, and maybe a bit more if I heard Hollis was losing contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear the boss is having a meeting you're not in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first sign be that Hollis was in trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hollis stopping the Friday doughnuts, probably. No, really, it'd be fewer school jobs in summer. If the councils start giving the big contracts to a company with robots, we'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving to a bigger firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I know everyone at Hollis, I know which van has the bad clutch. Starting again somewhere big doesn't appeal.

S1.say: I'd say some changes will be sensible and some silly, and we'll see which is which. I'm not against it, just not first in the queue.
S1.think: Refurbishing old, crooked buildings will take machines a long time to manage. Her real worry is her small family employer being squeezed by big firms with machines.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and keeps working, picking up new gadgets only if she must. Saves the same amount, more if she hears her employer is losing contracts.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing the boss is in a meeting she's not part of.
S1.quote: Mr Hollis stopping the Friday doughnuts, probably.
S1.fieldNote: Yara's worry attaches to her employer, not the technology itself. She wants to stay where she knows everyone, even down to which van has the bad clutch. Her centre outlook shows as a shrug: some good, some silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing hands-on work. That's... no, that's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't really know what to think, and I don't think anybody does. Somebody in charge needs to sort out what happens to people's jobs. I'm not one for marches but I'd want to hear a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be scared. I never learned anything except carpentry, and I don't use those tools, so I'd be starting from the very bottom. Kerem's job would probably go too, because driving's an obvious one for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't needed, the takeaways, the new sofa we were looking at. We'd move everything to savings and keep the car going instead of replacing it. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move in with them for a while if both our jobs went, to make the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn the AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, I'd have to. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it. In two years I'd maybe get to the level my little brother is at now, and by then it wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving in with your parents mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would feel like going backwards. We've had our own place for four years. But my mum's house has a spare room and she'd love it, so at least there's that.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know what to think and I doubt anyone does, and somebody in charge needs a plan for people's jobs. I'm not one for marches but I'd want to hear one.
S2.think: She'd be scared, because carpentry is all she knows and she'd be starting from the bottom with tools she doesn't use. Her partner's bus-driving job would probably go too.
S2.do: Cuts all unneeded spending, including takeaways and a planned new sofa, and keeps the old car going. Talks to her parents about moving in if both jobs go, to stretch the savings.
S2.feel: Alarmed; her stomach drops just saying it.
S2.quote: In two years I'd maybe get to the level my little brother is at now, and by then it wouldn't matter.
S2.fieldNote: For a resistant person, the two-year picture leaves no time to catch up, and Yara knows it. Her savings help, but the prospect of two incomes going at once frightens her. Family, not government, is her real fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Not much, but a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so the government and the companies should sit down and work out what happens to workers. I'd say people should start saving, because that's what I'd be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think about jobs that might last longest. The council has building maintenance teams for schools, and those feel safer to me, steady and boring. I'd be thirty-two, and I could do that kind of work for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe a third of my pay, so we'd have two years put away. In the second or third year I'd apply for a council maintenance job, because it's secure and has a pension. Mostly I'd keep my head down and see how it went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd feel like I had at least a bit of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the council job be safe from robots, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I suppose not forever. But councils are slow, and I'd rather be somewhere slow. It would buy me some years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the saving, mainly. With five years I could save a real pile, and it'd be okay if I was out of work for a year or two. With two years, I'm just scared.

S3.say: I'd say there are five years, so government and companies should sit down and work out what happens to workers. I'd tell people to start saving, because that's what I'd do.
S3.think: She'd look for work that lasts longest, like the council's school maintenance teams, which feel steady and boring. At 32 she could do that for a while.
S3.do: Saves about a third of her pay to build two years of savings, and applies for a council maintenance job with a pension in the second or third year. Otherwise keeps her head down and watches.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with at least a bit of a plan.
S3.quote: But councils are slow, and I'd rather be somewhere slow.
S3.fieldNote: Yara uses extra time to save and to move towards slower, safer employers rather than to learn new things. She sees the council job won't last forever but values the buffer. Her plan is about money and stability, not skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort things out properly, and nobody should panic. I'd want the people in charge to make a sensible plan. I'd probably say that to my mum, who'd be worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be okay. Ten more years at Hollis or the council, saving all the way, and we'd have a lot in the bank by thirty-seven. I'd worry a bit about what happens after, but that's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the same as now and keep saving steadily. Maybe Kerem and I would buy a small flat, because ten years of mortgage payments is a good chunk paid off. I'd keep an eye on the news and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The end point is the same. Doesn't that weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a little, when I think about it. But I don't like thinking about things ten years away, I've never been like that. I'll worry about it when I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of those ten years to learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe near the end, if I had to. I'd rather not. I know that sounds stubborn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort things out properly and nobody should panic. I'd want people in charge to make a sensible plan, and I'd tell my worried mum the same.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be okay, with ten more years of work and saving leaving a lot in the bank by 37. She'd worry a little about what comes after, but it feels far away.
S4.do: Keeps working as now and keeps saving steadily, and might buy a small flat with her partner. Watches the news and waits.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, because it's far enough away.
S4.quote: I'll worry about it when I can see it.
S4.fieldNote: Yara treats the decade as distance rather than preparation time. She admits she'd rather not learn anything new and calls it stubborn herself. Her calm here rests on savings and a habit of not looking far ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is some kind of income while you find your feet, and someone actually showing people like me what to do next, slowly, in person, not on an app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the schools. I've fixed classrooms where my own teachers taught me. I'd like to think a kid would still notice a door that someone cared about.

headlineQuote: I've fixed classrooms where my own teachers taught me.
portrait: Yara Yilmaz is a 27-year-old carpenter at a small family builder that refurbishes schools and clinics, living with her partner Kerem, a bus driver, with about eight months saved. She keeps a paper diary, never uses AI and has no wish to start. Her worries centre on her employer and her household rather than on politics. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both incomes could go and she'd be starting from the bottom; with more time she simply saves harder and looks for slower, safer employers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be starting from the bottom with no time and her partner's job could go too.
whatWouldHelp: Some income while people find their feet, and someone showing her what to do next, slowly and in person rather than on an app.
